title: Jiu-Jitsu and Job Hunting
html:
In my last post, I said that I needed to go for a long walk, and that I’d let you know what I figured out.

Well… I’ve done some figuring.

The job market is in rough shape.

I’m sure this comes as news to absolutely nobody, but it’s especially relevant to me as I wrap up graduate school. I’m a classic example of being over-credentialed and under-skilled, so I’ve gotten almost no traction during my job searching.

I know a little about a lot because I’ve been exposed to a lot while pursuing a BS in Computer Science and Neurobiology and an MS in Biomedical Data Science. But employers don’t care. Nor should they, really. They don’t care that I have a good GPA or that I’m a published author in academic journals. They only care about whether I can solve problems for them that are worth the cost of my salary and training. But, to do that, I need specific skills, something that higher education fails to cultivate in sufficient quantities.

The tension between exploration and exploitation, i.e., cultivating general vs. specific skills, exists in all areas of life. Training jiu-jitsu has forced me to conclude that specific skills always win, on the mats and in the workforce. To make myself a dangerous applicant, I need to follow the same principle that makes a dangerous grappler: Specificity.

“I fear not the man who has practiced 10,000 kicks once, but I fear the man who has practiced one kick 10,000 times.” — Bruce Lee

The fastest way to make yourself a dangerous grappler is to learn the ins and outs of a small number of positions, while learning just enough about a large number of positions to be able to defend yourself against them. If done properly, you’ll be able to reliably pull your opponent into where you’re most effective, then apply to your specific skills, the “kicks” you’ve practiced 10,000 times, to submit them.

The job market works the same. Employers do not want the applicant who has dabbled in 10,000 skills for an hour. They want the applicant who has spent 10,000 hours developing one skill.

So what does this mean for me?

It means playtime is over.

I need to make myself dangerous.
